items.readable_text:
Content:
Let [MATH: X] be an [MATH: n \times m] observation matrix with standardized data, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

Content:
Suppose we have the following singular value decomposition (SVD) of [MATH: X{:}]

Content:
[MATH: X = U \Sigma V^T]

Content:
Note that in the SVD, the columns of [MATH: U] are orthonormal, which implies that [MATH: U^T U = I] (the identity matrix).

Content:
Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of [MATH: X] can be derived as follows:

Content:
[MATH: C|= (1)/(n − 1)X^{T}X; = (1)/(n − 1)(UΣV^{T})^{T}(UΣV^{T}); = (1)/(n − 1)(VΣ^{T}U^{T})(UΣV^{T}); = (1)/(n − 1)VΣ^{T}(U^{T}U)_(⏟)_(I)ΣV^{T}; = V((1)/(n − 1)Σ^{T}Σ)V^{T}.]

Content:
The expression [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma] represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.]

Content:
Now, notice the following:

Content:
- The matrix [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma] is a diagonal [MATH: m \times m] matrix with the eigenvalues of [MATH: C] (in descending order) on the main diagonal.
- The matrix [MATH: V] is an [MATH: m \times m] matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of [MATH: C.]

Content:
To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix [MATH: X,] the columns of the matrix [MATH: V] in the SVD are the principal components of the data.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [MATH: C] are called the principal components of the data. If

[MATH: \lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \lambda_3]

are the eigenvalues of [MATH: C] written in descending order, then:

  • the [MATH: 1]st principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] corresponding to the [MATH: 1]st eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_1,]

  • the [MATH: 2]nd principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] corresponding to the [MATH: 2]nd eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2,]

  • the [MATH: 3]rd principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_3] corresponding to the [MATH: 3]rd eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_3.]

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to [MATH: X] is

[MATH: C|= (1)/(n − 1)X^{T}X; = (1)/(n − 1)(UΣV^{T})^{T}(UΣV^{T}); = (1)/(n − 1)VΣ^{T}(U^{T}U)ΣV^{T}; = V((1)/(n − 1)Σ^{T}Σ)V^{T},]

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.] Notice the following:

  • The matrix [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma] is a diagonal [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.]

  • The matrix [MATH: V] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.]

Therefore, the columns of [MATH: V] are the principal components of the data. So, the third principal component is

[MATH: [(1)/(3); − (2)/(3); (2)/(3)]]

items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose we have a sample of [MATH: n] observations, where each observation has [MATH: m] features. We store this data in the [MATH: n \times m] observation matrix [MATH: X,] where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

Content:
[MATH: [x_{11}|x_{12}|…|x_{1m}; x_{21}|x_{22}|…|x_{2m}; ⋮|⋮|⋱|⋮; x_{n1}|x_{n2}|…|x_{nm}]]

Content:
We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let [MATH: \mathbf{x}_j] denote the [MATH: j]th column of [MATH: X.] The sample covariance matrix, [MATH: C_X,] is given by

Content:
[MATH: [Var[x_{1}]|…|Cov[x_{1}, x_{m}]; ⋮|⋱|⋮; Cov[x_{m}, x_{1}]|…|Var[x_{m}]]]

Content:
The total variance of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of [MATH: C_X] (the trace of the matrix). That is,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Total Variance} = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m].]

Content:
How is the total variance related to the singular values of [MATH: X?]

Content:
We recall that using the singular value decomposition [MATH: X = U \Sigma V^T,] the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m] of [MATH: C_X] are related to the singular values [MATH: \sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m] of [MATH: X] by:

Content:
[MATH: \lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for } i=1,\ldots,m.]

Content:
Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance.

items.readable_text:
Content:
To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables [MATH: Y = XV.] The covariance of [MATH: Y] is given by

Content:
[MATH: C_{Y} = (1)/(n − 1)Y^{T}Y = (1)/(n − 1)(XV)^{T}(XV) = V^{T}((1)/(n − 1)X^{T}X)_(⏟)_(C_{X})V.]

Content:
Since [MATH: V] contains the eigenvectors of [MATH: C_X,] the matrix [MATH: C_Y] is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_i] of [MATH: C_X{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [λ_{1}|…|0; ⋮|⋱|⋮; 0|…|λ_{m}]]

Content:
The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like [MATH: Y=XV.] Therefore, the total variance of [MATH: Y] is the same as the total variance of [MATH: X{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: \lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},] we conclude that the total variance is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

Content:
[MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.}]

Content:
Let's see an example.

items.readable_text:
Content:
A nutritionist measured [MATH: 3] features among a group of clients:

Content:
- body mass index ([MATH: x_1])
- height ([MATH: x_2])
- weight ([MATH: x_3])

Content:
The collected data was stored in the mean-centered observation matrix [MATH: X,] where each row contains measurements for a particular client. The nutritionist finds that the singular values of [MATH: X] are

Content:
[MATH: \sigma_1=12, \qquad \sigma_2=5, \qquad \sigma_3=4.]

Content:
The nutritionist then decides to reduce the dimensionality of the data set. To do this, they convert the original observation matrix [MATH: X] into a new matrix [MATH: Y] using the equation

Content:
[MATH: Y = X V_1,]

Content:
where [MATH: V_1] is the [MATH: 3 \times 1] matrix containing the first principal component of the data only. As a result, [MATH: Y] is an [MATH: n \times 1] matrix that gives a single feature associated with each client.

Content:
What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix [MATH: Y] compared to the initial observation matrix [MATH: X?]

Content:
The total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

Content:
[MATH: Total|∝∑_(i = 1)^(3)σ_{i}^{2}; = (12)^{2} + (5)^{2} + (4)^{2}; = 185.]

Content:
Since the nutritionist used only the first principal component, the preserved variance is

Content:
[MATH: Preserved|∝∑_(i = 1)^(1)σ_{i}^{2}; = (12)^{2}; = 144.]

Content:
Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

Content:
[MATH: (Preserved)/(Total)|= (144)/(185); ≈ 0.778; = 77.8 %.]

Content:
To summarize:

Content:
- The nutritionist reduced the dimensionality of the data from [MATH: 3] (initially, each client had three features) to just [MATH: 1] (only one feature characterizes each client after the transformation).
- In doing so, [MATH: 77.8\%] of the variance is preserved in the transformed data.

Let [MATH: V] be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

[MATH: Y = XV]

we can convert our observation matrix [MATH: X] into a new matrix [MATH: Y] of (linearly) transformed observations such that

  • the covariance matrix of [MATH: Y] is diagonal (meaning that the new features [MATH: y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_5] are uncorrelated),

  • the features [MATH: y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_5] are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and

  • the squares of the singular values [MATH: \sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2, \ldots, \sigma_5^2] represent the variances in the respective features [MATH: y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_5.]

Now, the total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

[MATH: Total|∝∑_(i = 1)^(5)σ_{i}^{2}; = (7)^{2} + (5)^{2} + (3)^{2} + (2)^{2} + (1)^{2}; = 88]

Since the analyst used only the first two principal components, the remaining variance is

[MATH: Remaining|∝∑_(i = 1)^(2)σ_{i}^{2}; = (7)^{2} + (5)^{2}; = 74.]

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

[MATH: (Remaining)/(Total)|= (74)/(88); ≈ 0.841; = 84.1%.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Let [MATH: X] be an [MATH: n \times m] observation matrix with standardized data, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

Content:
Suppose we have the following singular value decomposition (SVD) of [MATH: X{:}]

Content:
[MATH: X = U \Sigma V^T]

Content:
Note that in the SVD, the columns of [MATH: U] are orthonormal, which implies that [MATH: U^T U = I] (the identity matrix).

Content:
Using this decomposition, the sample covariance matrix of [MATH: X] can be derived as follows:

Content:
[MATH: C|= (1)/(n − 1)X^{T}X; = (1)/(n − 1)(UΣV^{T})^{T}(UΣV^{T}); = (1)/(n − 1)(VΣ^{T}U^{T})(UΣV^{T}); = (1)/(n − 1)VΣ^{T}(U^{T}U)_(⏟)_(I)ΣV^{T}; = V((1)/(n − 1)Σ^{T}Σ)V^{T}.]

Content:
The expression [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma] represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.]

Content:
Now, notice the following:

Content:
- The matrix [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma] is a diagonal [MATH: m \times m] matrix with the eigenvalues of [MATH: C] (in descending order) on the main diagonal.
- The matrix [MATH: V] is an [MATH: m \times m] matrix whose columns are the unit eigenvectors of [MATH: C.]

Content:
To summarize, if we write down the singular value decomposition of the standardized observation matrix [MATH: X,] the columns of the matrix [MATH: V] in the SVD are the principal components of the data.

---

Item 2 — Example: Finding a Principal Component from SVD

Example Prompt:
[MATH: [(2)/(sqrt(5))|− (1)/(sqrt(5)); (1)/(sqrt(5))|(2)/(sqrt(5))]]
Consider the matrices [MATH: U] and [MATH: V] above. Let [MATH: X] be a [MATH: 2 \times 3] standardized observation matrix, where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature. Given that [MATH: X = U \Sigma V^T] is a singular value decomposition of [MATH: X,] what is the third principal component of the data?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Recall that the unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [MATH: C] are called the principal components of the data. If

[MATH: \lambda_1 \gt \lambda_2 \gt \lambda_3]

are the eigenvalues of [MATH: C] written in descending order, then:

- the [MATH: 1]st principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] corresponding to the [MATH: 1]st eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_1,]
- the [MATH: 2]nd principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] corresponding to the [MATH: 2]nd eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_2,]
- the [MATH: 3]rd principal component is the unit eigenvector [MATH: \mathbf{v}_3] corresponding to the [MATH: 3]rd eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda_3.]

Notice that the covariance matrix corresponding to [MATH: X] is

[MATH: C|= (1)/(n − 1)X^{T}X; = (1)/(n − 1)(UΣV^{T})^{T}(UΣV^{T}); = (1)/(n − 1)VΣ^{T}(U^{T}U)ΣV^{T}; = V((1)/(n − 1)Σ^{T}Σ)V^{T},]

where the final expression represents the diagonal form of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.] Notice the following:

- The matrix [MATH: \dfrac{1}{n-1}\Sigma^T \Sigma] is a diagonal [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, where the entries on the main diagonal are the eigenvalues (written in descending order) of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.]
- The matrix [MATH: V] is a [MATH: 3 \times 3] matrix, whose columns are the corresponding unit eigenvectors of the covariance matrix [MATH: C.]

Therefore, the columns of [MATH: V] are the principal components of the data.
So, the third principal component is

[MATH: [(1)/(3); − (2)/(3); (2)/(3)]]

---

Item 5 — Tutorial: Total Variance of the Observation Matrix

Content:
Suppose we have a sample of [MATH: n] observations, where each observation has [MATH: m] features. We store this data in the [MATH: n \times m] observation matrix [MATH: X,] where each row represents one observation and each column represents one feature.

Content:
[MATH: [x_{11}|x_{12}|…|x_{1m}; x_{21}|x_{22}|…|x_{2m}; ⋮|⋮|⋱|⋮; x_{n1}|x_{n2}|…|x_{nm}]]

Content:
We assume the data has been mean-centered. Let [MATH: \mathbf{x}_j] denote the [MATH: j]th column of [MATH: X.] The sample covariance matrix, [MATH: C_X,] is given by

Content:
[MATH: [Var[x_{1}]|…|Cov[x_{1}, x_{m}]; ⋮|⋱|⋮; Cov[x_{m}, x_{1}]|…|Var[x_{m}]]]

Content:
The total variance of the observed data equals the sum of the entries on the leading diagonal of [MATH: C_X] (the trace of the matrix). That is,

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Total Variance} = \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_1] + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_2] + \cdots + \textrm{Var}[\mathbf{x}_m].]

Content:
How is the total variance related to the singular values of [MATH: X?]

Content:
We recall that using the singular value decomposition [MATH: X = U \Sigma V^T,] the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1,\ldots, \lambda_m] of [MATH: C_X] are related to the singular values [MATH: \sigma_1,\ldots, \sigma_m] of [MATH: X] by:

Content:
[MATH: \lambda_i = \dfrac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1} \quad \text{for } i=1,\ldots,m.]

Content:
Next, we will use this relationship to compute the total variance.

---

Item 6 — Tutorial: Finding the Total Variance

Content:
To find the total variance in terms of singular values, define the change of variables [MATH: Y = XV.] The covariance of [MATH: Y] is given by

Content:
[MATH: C_{Y} = (1)/(n − 1)Y^{T}Y = (1)/(n − 1)(XV)^{T}(XV) = V^{T}((1)/(n − 1)X^{T}X)_(⏟)_(C_{X})V.]

Content:
Since [MATH: V] contains the eigenvectors of [MATH: C_X,] the matrix [MATH: C_Y] is diagonal and contains the eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_i] of [MATH: C_X{:}]

Content:
[MATH: [λ_{1}|…|0; ⋮|⋱|⋮; 0|…|λ_{m}]]

Content:
The total variance is defined as the trace (sum of diagonal elements) of the covariance matrix. A key property of the trace is that it is invariant under orthogonal transformations like [MATH: Y=XV.] Therefore, the total variance of [MATH: Y] is the same as the total variance of [MATH: X{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \textrm{Total Variance} = \text{Tr}(C_X) = \text{Tr}(C_Y) = \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i.]

Content:
Substituting [MATH: \lambda_i = \frac{\sigma_i^2}{n-1},] we conclude that the total variance is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

Content:
[MATH: \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{\textrm{Total Variance} \:\propto\: \sum_{i=1}^m \sigma^2_i.}]

Content:
Let's see an example.

---

Item 7 — Tutorial: Computing the Remaining Variance After Dimensionality Reduction

Content:
A nutritionist measured [MATH: 3] features among a group of clients:

Content:
- body mass index ([MATH: x_1])
- height ([MATH: x_2])
- weight ([MATH: x_3])

Content:
The collected data was stored in the mean-centered observation matrix [MATH: X,] where each row contains measurements for a particular client. The nutritionist finds that the singular values of [MATH: X] are

Content:
[MATH: \sigma_1=12, \qquad \sigma_2=5, \qquad \sigma_3=4.]

Content:
The nutritionist then decides to reduce the dimensionality of the data set. To do this, they convert the original observation matrix [MATH: X] into a new matrix [MATH: Y] using the equation

Content:
[MATH: Y = X V_1,]

Content:
where [MATH: V_1] is the [MATH: 3 \times 1] matrix containing the first principal component of the data only. As a result, [MATH: Y] is an [MATH: n \times 1] matrix that gives a single feature associated with each client.

Content:
What percentage of the original variance is preserved in the new transformed matrix [MATH: Y] compared to the initial observation matrix [MATH: X?]

Content:
The total variance over all features is proportional to the sum of the squared singular values:

Content:
[MATH: Total|∝∑_(i = 1)^(3)σ_{i}^{2}; = (12)^{2} + (5)^{2} + (4)^{2}; = 185.]

Content:
Since the nutritionist used only the first principal component, the preserved variance is

Content:
[MATH: Preserved|∝∑_(i = 1)^(1)σ_{i}^{2}; = (12)^{2}; = 144.]

Content:
Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

Content:
[MATH: (Preserved)/(Total)|= (144)/(185); ≈ 0.778; = 77.8 %.]

Content:
To summarize:

Content:
- The nutritionist reduced the dimensionality of the data from [MATH: 3] (initially, each client had three features) to just [MATH: 1] (only one feature characterizes each client after the transformation).
- In doing so, [MATH: 77.8\%] of the variance is preserved in the transformed data.

Item 8 — Example: Finding the Variance from SVD

Let [MATH: V] be the matrix of principal components. Then, applying the change of variables

[MATH: Y = XV]

we can convert our observation matrix [MATH: X] into a new matrix [MATH: Y] of (linearly) transformed observations such that

- the covariance matrix of [MATH: Y] is diagonal (meaning that the new features [MATH: y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_5] are uncorrelated),
- the features [MATH: y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_5] are arranged in order of decreasing variance, and
- the squares of the singular values [MATH: \sigma_1^2, \sigma_2^2, \ldots, \sigma_5^2] represent the variances in the respective features [MATH: y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_5.]

[MATH: Total|∝∑_(i = 1)^(5)σ_{i}^{2}; = (7)^{2} + (5)^{2} + (3)^{2} + (2)^{2} + (1)^{2}; = 88]

Since the analyst used only the first two principal components, the remaining variance is

[MATH: Remaining|∝∑_(i = 1)^(2)σ_{i}^{2}; = (7)^{2} + (5)^{2}; = 74.]

Therefore, our required percentage can be computed as

[MATH: (Remaining)/(Total)|= (74)/(88); ≈ 0.841; = 84.1%.]
